before: A Git branch is a name that points to a commit. Creating a branch does not copy your project into a second folder.
When you switch branches, Git makes that branch current. Make sure existing changes are saved safely before switching.
A commit made on a feature branch advances that branch. It does not move main automatically.

Create greeting.txt containing the single line Hello in a new disposable practice folder first. With Git configured there, create a starting commit:
```bash
git init -b main
git add greeting.txt
git commit -m "Add first greeting"
```
Run these commands only in that new practice folder, never in an unrelated repository.

Create and switch to a feature branch.
```bash
git switch -c friendly-greeting
```

Change the file to Hello, explorer and save it. Commit on the current branch.
```bash
git add greeting.txt
git commit -m "Make the greeting friendlier"
```

Switch back to main and inspect greeting.txt. It still contains Hello because main has not moved.
```bash
git switch main
git status
```

Merge the feature branch into the current main branch.
```bash
git merge friendly-greeting
git log --oneline --all --graph
```
In this simple history, main moves forward to the feature commit. The file now contains Hello, explorer.
If both branches edit the same lines differently, Git may ask you to resolve a conflict. Review both intentions, edit the file into the wanted result, test it, then stage and commit the resolution.
This displays Hi then Hello. Reading one saved entry does not replace the other.
Passing this JavaScript check does not prove you created Git branches. Confirm the real walkthrough separately by inspecting the file before and after the merge.
after: A Git branch is a name pointing to a commit. Making a branch does not make a second project folder.
Switching chooses the branch to work on. Save or safely set aside existing edits before switching.
A new commit moves the current branch forward. It does not automatically move main.

In a new disposable folder, make greeting.txt containing Hello. Run git init -b main. Set a local Git author name and email if needed. Then run git add greeting.txt and git commit -m "Add first greeting".
Use this new practice folder for the walkthrough. Keep unrelated projects untouched.
Run git switch -c friendly-greeting. This creates the branch and makes it current.
Change greeting.txt to Hello, explorer and save it. Run git add greeting.txt, then git commit -m "Make the greeting friendlier".
Run git switch main. Open greeting.txt: it still says Hello because main still points to the first commit.
While on main, run git merge friendly-greeting. This brings that branch's change into main.
In this simple history, main moves forward to the new commit. greeting.txt now says Hello, explorer. Use git log --oneline --all --graph to inspect the history.
A conflict means Git cannot combine some changes on its own. Read both intended changes, edit the wanted result, test it, then stage and commit the resolution.
Reading saved["draft"].code does not change saved["main"].code. This models choosing a version; it does not run Git.

before.question: You branch from main, commit a new greeting on draft, then switch to main without merging. Which greeting is on main?
choices: The old greeting from main’s commit.
The new greeting because every commit updates every branch.
before.explanation: The commit advanced draft, not main. Switching to main selects its earlier commit. A later merge is a separate action.

after.question: You commit a new greeting on draft, then switch to main without merging. Which greeting is on main?
choices: The old greeting from main's commit.
The new greeting, because every commit moves every branch.
after.explanation: Only draft moved to the new commit. main keeps its earlier version until a separate change moves it.
